extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (practitioners and scholars assessing or litigating patent damages)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for proving, measuring, and computing damages and profits in patent-infringement cases, including evidentiary rules, apportionment when a patent covers only part of an article, and effects of a damages judgment on future rights. Focused on U.S. common-law principles as explained in a treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual damages must be proved; defendant's profits are indirect evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Actual damages must be actually proved, and cannot be assumed as a 'imaginary' legal inference from any facts.' The profits made by the defendant on infringing articles 'tends to show the amount of the plaintiff's loss.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant's profits may be admitted as indirect evidence of plaintiff's loss but are not conclusive. Courts will not assume plaintiff would have made all sales the defendant made; connecting facts (readiness to supply market, those customers would have bought of plaintiff, comparable manufacturing/marketing expense) must be established before presuming plaintiff would have made defendant's profits. (See Seymour v. McCormick; multiple cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of profits: cost vs yield and items to include
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The profits arising from the sale of a patented article are represented by the difference between cost and yield.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In estimating cost include expense for materials and interest thereon, price paid for labor in making and selling, manufacturer's profit on materials and labor, rental value of factory or store, and other items a manufacturer ordinarily reckons among business expenses; bad debts are usually included. Yield is the price obtained by the infringer. Use gross prices and expenses (books of account, witness testimony) to calculate actual profits. See §§1138–1143 for further items and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment when the patent covers only a part of an article
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Where the patent covers only a portion of the article ... the profit due to the incorporation of the improvement into the article must be separated from the profit which would have been received by the defendant had this portion been omitted, and the latter profit be excluded from the computation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the entire value of the defendant's device flows from the plaintiff's invention, the entire profits belong to the plaintiff; otherwise profits must be apportioned. If the defendant's device is unsalable without the patented portion, the entire profit may be regarded as derived from the invention. Where separation is impossible because of confusion, courts may treat the whole profit as from the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must prove what portion of profits are due to his invention (or unsalability without it)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That the plaintiff must prove what portion of the profits are due to his invention, or else that the defendant's device is unsalable without it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence as to the special value of the part used by the infringer is required unless the rest is without value. Demonstrate relative value by introducing evidence comparing the machine (or article) with and without the improvement; show whether the machine stripped of improvements would be useless in the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages limited to value of the use of the improvement infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That the damages must be limited to the value of the use of the improvement infringed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patent covers only an improvement, the patentee's recovery should exclude mere manufacturing profits and exclude the value of the use of the old machine; measure damages by the advantage or benefit from the use of the improvement (i.e., the additional value conferred by the improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: When patentee enjoys monopoly by manufacture and sale, defendant's profits are an important indication but other elements must be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: 'When the exclusive use ... consists in the manufacture and sale of the patented invention, indirect evidence of the loss is afforded by the profits made by the defendant upon his unlawful sales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other elements—injury to plaintiff's own business by depreciation of demand or prices—must be shown by direct evidence. The defendant's profits form one element; plaintiff should also prove lost sales, reduced prices, or other business injuries to fully measure damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that plaintiff would have supplied the market permits presumption he would have made defendant's profits
rubrics_metrics.description: 'When it is proved that the plaintiff was ready and able to supply the market, that those who would have been his customers have bought of the defendant, and that his expense in manufacturing and marketing the patented articles would not have exceeded that incurred by the defendant, it may safely be presumed that but for the infringement he would have made the profits which have been received by the defendant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish readiness/capacity to supply, identity or substitution of customers, and comparable costs; once those connecting facts are established, defendant's profits become strong evidence of plaintiff's loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot assume plaintiff would have sold all defendant sold (quality/price differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It cannot be assumed that the plaintiff would have sold all the defendant sold, especially where defendant's articles are cheaper and of poorer quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant's product was cheaper or inferior, the jury should not automatically equate defendant's sales with lost plaintiff sales; must consider diversion of custom and other circumstantial evidence. Jury may infer lost sales from diversion of custom but must weigh market realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury may infer from circumstances (diversion of custom) plaintiff would have made sales but for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The jury may infer from circumstances such as diversion of custom, &c., that the plaintiff would have made the sales but for the infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstantial evidence (customer testimony, market behavior, timing of sales) can support inference of lost sales; such inferences may obviate the need for detailed profit-accounting in some cases (see Covert v. Sargent and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only actual profits received by defendant are generally admissible (not speculative gains by diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The amount is governed by the profits the defendant actually made ... the gain which the defendant might have made by diligence, etc., is no measure of the plaintiff's loss, though the actual gain might be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base damages on hypothetical higher profits the defendant could have realized with more skill or diligence; focus on actual receipts and expenditures. However, plaintiff may recover excess beyond defendant's profit if plaintiff would have earned higher profit under same sales conditions (proved disparity in cost or price).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles sold before patent issue cannot be counted in profits or damages
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That articles sold before the issue of the patent cannot be reckoned in account of profits or damages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales occurring prior to patent issuance are excluded from the damages accounting (see Lyon v. Donaldson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where defendant's device is useless without plaintiff's invention, entire profits are recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That where the defendant's device is useless without the plaintiff's, the entire profits are part of the damages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the infringing product would have been unsalable without the patented improvement, courts may attribute the whole profit to the infringement and award it to the patentee (cases: Zane v. Peck Bros., Carter v. Baker, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff cannot recover profits unless defendant actually made profits
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That the plaintiff cannot recover profits unless the defendant made profits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant derived no profit from the infringement, profit-based remedies are unavailable; recovery may be nominal if only the act of infringement is shown without demonstrable loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere making (without use or sale) usually yields only nominal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ordinarily, the mere making of the invention, without using or selling it, does not interfere with the plaintiff's enjoyment, and though an infringement of the patent is compensated for by nominal damages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mere manufacture without use/sale does not affect patentee's market enjoyment, damages will typically be nominal absent evidence of actual business injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: One who sells patented articles with intent they will be used to infringe is jointly liable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That one who makes and sells a patented invention, or the parts of a patented invention, with intent that the articles sold shall be used in violation of the patent, becomes thereby a joint tort-feasor with the actual users, and may be sued singly or together with them for the damages inflicted on the plaintiff.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A seller who intends infringement may be held responsible for damages caused by downstream users; sale price may be deemed to include the value of the infringing use. See sections on contributory infringement/joint tortfeasance (§§903,924 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: When defendant's infringing acts differ from plaintiff's monopoly practice, measure of damages depends on nature of act
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The acts of infringement performed by the defendant do not always correspond with those by which the plaintiff or his specific licensees enjoy the patented invention ... the loss sustained by the plaintiff must be determined in a different manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant makes and sells while plaintiff's monopoly is manufacture-and-sale, sale may affect plaintiff by putting invention into others' hands; if defendant only uses in his business, measure is the profit plaintiff would have made had defendant bought from him. Tailor proof to whether infringement is making-only, use-only, or sale to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering profits or damages does not necessarily vest title or a license to future use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A recovery of the profits for the use is but for a limited portion of the time ... the recovery of the established patent fee covers the entire value as fixed by the patentee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect of a damages judgment on defendant's future rights depends on measure chosen: if measure is an established license fee (a fixed patent fee covering term), satisfaction of judgment may entitle defendant to use for remainder of term; recovery of past profits typically compensates only for past infringement and does not license future use. If plaintiff preserved exclusive use, satisfaction of judgment gives no right to future use. Nominal-damage judgments do not operate as licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may look beyond defendant's profits to what plaintiff would fairly have earned
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They are not bound by the measure of the profits of the defendant, but have a right to look to the profits which the plaintiff or the patentee would have made under the circumstances, if not interfered with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows the plaintiff would have realized greater profit (e.g., lower costs or higher prices), the jury may award damages reflecting plaintiff's lost profit rather than strictly defendant's actual profit. Must be supported by evidence of plaintiff's likely returns absent infringement.
